और सक्षम प्राधिकारी ने, उक्त अधिनियम की धारा 6 की उपधारा () के अधीन केन्द्रीय सरकार को रिपोर्ट दे 
दी है; 


और केन्द्रीय सरकार ने, उक्त रिपोर्ट पर विचार करने के पश्चात, और यह समाधान हो जाने पर कि उक्त भूमि 
पाइपलाइन बिछाने के लिए अपेक्षित है, उसमें उपयोग के अधिकार का अर्जन करने का विनिश्चय किया है ; 


अतः अब, केन्द्रीय सरकार, उक्त अधिनियम की धारा 6 की उपधारा (॥) द्वारा प्रदत्त शक्तियों का प्रयोग करते 
हुए, यह घोषणा करती है कि इस अधिसूचना से संलग्न अनुसूची में विनिर्दिष्ट भूमि में पाइपलाइन बिछाने के लिए 
उपयोग के अधिकार का अर्जन किया जाए ; 

और केन्द्रीय सरकार उक्त अधिनियम की धारा 6 की उपधारा (4) द्वारा प्रदत्त शक्तियों का प्रयोग करते हुए, यह 
निर्देश देती है कि उक्त भूमि में उपयोग का अधिकार इस घोषणा के प्रकाशन की तारीख से केन्द्रीय सरकार में निहित 
होने के बजाए, सभी विल्लंगमों से मुक्त होकर हिन्दुस्तान पेट्रोलियम कॉर्पोरेशन लिमिटेड में निहित होगा।

MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS 
New Delhi, the |lth August, 2025 


S.O. 469.—Whereas, by the notification of the Government of India in the Ministry of Petroleum and 
Natural Gas, number S.O. 35(E) dated the 27th January, 2025, issued under sub-section (l) of section 3 of the 
Petroleum and Minerals Pipelines (Acquisition of Right of User in Land) Act, 962 (50 of 962) (hereinafter 
referred to as “the said Act’), and published in the Weekly Gazette of India dated January 26 — February |, 2025, 
the Central Government declared its intention to acquire the Right of User in the land specified in the Schedule 
appended to that notification, for the purpose of laying a pipeline for transportation of petroleum products from 
Visakha (Andhra Pradesh) to Raipur (Chhattisgarh) in the State of Andhra Pradesh by Hindustan Petroleum 
Corporation Limited; 


And whereas copies of the said Weekly Gazette notification were made available to the public on 28th 
April, 2025; 


And whereas the Competent Authority has, under sub-section (l) of section 6 of the said Act, submitted 
his report to the Central Government; 


And whereas the Central Government, after considering the said report and being satisfied that the said 
land is required for the purpose of laying the said pipeline, has decided to acquire the Right of User therein; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (l) of section 6 of the said Act, the 
Central Government hereby declares that the Right of User in the land specified in the Schedule appended to this 
notification is acquired for the purpose of laying the said pipeline; 


And further, in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (4) of section 6 of the said Act, the 
Central Government hereby directs that the Right of User in the said land for laying the pipeline shall, instead of 
vesting in the Central Government, vest on the date of publication of this declaration, in Hindustan Petroleum 
Corporation Limited, free from all encumbrances; 


Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited shall be exclusively liable for any compensation in terms of 
Section l0 of the said Act; 


Further, in accordance with Section [3 of the said Act, no suit, claim, or legal proceeding shall lie against the 
Central Government in respect of any matter relating to the said pipeline.

6. Issue No.II:- Undisputedly in the present matter Petitioner has been terminated from service vide order 
dated 9'" May 2008 and present industrial dispute has been raised by the Petitioner in the year 205 after seven 
years from the date of his termination, Petitioner has not furnished any explanation in his petition for such

In this context, reference of few decisions of Hon’ble Supreme Court are relevant as discussed hereunder:- 
In K R Reddy Vs. Industrial Tribunal-II, Hyderabad, Hon’ble Court held:- 


“The Supreme Court extensively considered the scope of relevant provisions and precedent decisions and held 
that there was inordinate, unexplained delay in referring the dispute.” 


In the case of Assistant Engineer, CAD, Kota and Dhan Kumwar, CA No.6473, 2006 III LLJ, the Hon'ble 
Apex Court have held: 


“workman raising the dispute eight years after termination of service —therefore relief by Labour Court should 
not have been granted to workman.” 


In Haryana State Co-operative Land Development Bank and Neelam, 2005 I LLJ, the Apex Court held: 


“Though no time limit prescribed for raising industrial dispute, but stale claim, could not be entertained - 
approaching Labour Court after delay of more than 7 years. Held:- justified refusal of relief in this case.” 


In the case of Sri Prabhakar Vs. Joint Director Sericulture Department in Civil Appeal decision dated 
7.9.I5 Hon'ble Apex Court have held:- 


“40) On the basis of aforesaid discussion, we summarise the legal position as under: 


“An industrial dispute has to be referred by the appropriate Government for adjudication and the workman 
cannot approach the Labour Court or Industrial Tribunal directly, except in those cases which are covered 
by Section 2A of the Act. Reference is made under Section 70 of the Act in those cases where the appropriate 
Government forms an opinion that ‘any industrial dispute exists or is apprehended’. The words ‘industrial 
dispute exists’ are of paramount importance unless there is an existence of an industrial dispute (or the 
dispute is apprehended or it is apprehended such a dispute may arise in near future), no reference is to be 
made. Thus, existence or apprehension of an industrial dispute is a sine qua non for making the reference. 
No doubt, at the time of taking a decision whether a reference is to be made or not, the appropriate 
Government is not to go into the merits of the dispute. Making of reference is only an administrative 
function. At the same time, on the basis of material on record, satisfaction of the existence of the industrial 
dispute or the apprehension of an industrial dispute is necessary. Such existence/apprehension of industrial 
dispute, thus, becomes a condition precedent, though it will be only subjective satisfaction based on material 
on record. Since, we are not concerned with the satisfaction dealing with cases where there is apprehended 
industrial dispute, discussion that follows would confine to existence of an industrial dispute. Dispute or 
difference arises when one party make a demand and other party rejects the same. It is held by this Court in 
number of cases that before raising the industrial dispute making of demand is a necessary pre-condition. In 
such a scenario, if the services of a workman are terminated and he does not make the demand and/or raise 
the issue alleging wrongful termination immediately thereafter or within reasonable time and raises the 
same after considerable lapse of period, whether it can be said that industrial dispute still exist. Since there 
is no period of limitation, it gives right to the workman to raise the dispute even belatedly. However, if the 
dispute is raised after a long period, it has to be seen as to whether such a dispute still exists? Thus, 
notwithstanding the fact that law of limitation does not apply, it is to be shown by the workman that there is 
a dispute in praesenti. For this purpose, he has to demonstrate that even if considerable period has lapsed 
and there are laches and delays, such delay has not resulted into making the industrial dispute seized to 
exist. Therefore, if the workman is able to give satisfactory explanation for these laches and delays and 
demonstrate that the circumstances discloses that issue is still alive, delay would not come in his way 
because of the reason that law of limitation has no application. On the other hand, if because of such delay 
dispute no longer remains alive and is to be treated as “dead”, then it would be non-existent dispute which 
cannot be referred. Take, for example, a case where the workman issues notice after his termination, 


[भाग Il—ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त 6, 2025/श्रावण 25, 947 568 


questioning the termination and demanding reinstatement. He is able to show that there were discussions 
from time to time and the parties were trying to sort out the matter amicably. Or he is able to show that there 
were assurances by the Management to the effect that he would be taken back in service and because of these 
reasons, he did not immediately raise the dispute by approaching the labour authorities seeking reference or 
did not invoke the remedy under Section 2A of the Act. In such a scenario, it can be treated that the dispute 
was live and existing as the workman never abandoned his right. However, in this very example, even if the 
notice of demand was sent but it did not evoke any positive response or there was specific rejection by the 
Management of his demand contained in the notice and thereafter he sleeps over the matter for number of 
years, it can be treated that he accepted the factum of his termination and rejection thereof by the 
Management and acquiesced into the said rejection. Take another example. A workman approaches the Civil 
Court by filing a suit against his termination which was pending for number of years and was ultimately 
dismissed on the ground that Civil Court did not have jurisdiction to enforce the contract of personal service 
and does not grant any reinstatement. At that stage, when the suit is dismissed or he withdraws that suit and 
then involves the machinery under the Act, it can lead to the conclusion that dispute is still alive as the 
workman had not accepted the termination but was agitating the same; albeit in a wrong forum. In contrast, 
in those cases where there was no agitation by the workman against his termination and the dispute is raised 
belatedly and the delay or laches remain unexplained, it would be presumed that he had waived his right or 
acquiesced into the act of termination and, therefore, at the time when the dispute is raised it had become 
stale and was not an ‘existing dispute’. In such circumstances, the appropriate Government can refuse to 
make reference. In the alternative, the Labour Court/Industrial Court can also hold that there is no 
“industrial dispute” within the meaning of Section 2(k) of the Act and, therefore, no relief can be granted. 


447) We may hasten to clarify that in those cases where the Court finds that dispute still existed, though raised 
belatedly, it is always permissible for the Court to take the aspect of delay into consideration and mould the relief. 
In such cases, it is still open for the Court to either grant reinstatement without back wages or lesser back wages 
or grant compensation instead of reinstatement. We are of the opinion that the law on this issue has to be applied 
in the aforesaid perspective in such matters.” 


Moreover, in the case of Chief Engineer (Construction) Vs. Keshav Rao, 2005 JCR 96, Hon’ble Supreme 
Court have held that, the delay of a one year and five months in issuing a notice appears to us to be significant. 
Here, in the present matter workman has not issued any notice or raised dispute against his termination in any 
forum for a long period of about fourteen years and his claim against dismissal has become stale due to inordinate 
delay and latches. 


Vs Therefore, in view of the fore gone discussion and law laid down by the Hon'ble Apex Court, in the 
instant case industrial dispute has been raised by Workman in the year 20I5 against his termination order dated 
7/i9.5.2008 after a lapse of 7 years and has not furnished any explanation for such inordinate delay. Thus, the 
present dispute of Petitioner against termination order has become stale and not maintainable. Therefore, the 
petition filed by the Workman is not maintainable due to inordinate delay and latches and such a dispute has 
become stale and hence not maintainable. 


This issue is decided against the Workman and in favour of the Respondent.

9. In view of the submissions made by either parties perused the record of enquiry proceedings. Record of 
enquiry proceeding goes to reveal that Petitioner was served with chargesheet dated 9.2.2008 and wherein it is 
alleged against CSE workman that he has put in only 68 days musters for !90 musters in a calendar year 2007. 
Further, said record goes to show that the management has examined two witnesses during the enquiry proceeding 
in support of the charge and management witnesses has given the evidence that the Workman remained habitually 
absent from duty unauthorisedly without sanction of leave and he has put in only 68 musters in the year 2007. 
Although, the CSE Workman was accorded cross examination from these witnesses opportunity but he did not 
avail of it. The statement of the CSE Workman was recorded during Enquiry and in his statement Workman has 
admitted that he was absent from duty on the number of days mentioned in the charge sheet during the year 2007 
but he was absent from duty due to ill-health and elder father (uncle) expired. Further, workman stated that he did 
not report at company’s hospital for treatment or for sick, unfit and he do not have any record to defend his case. 
Further, in cross examination CSE Workman states that he did not apply for leave, sick or send information about 
his absence from duty to the management and did not report sick at company’s hospital for treatment for sick, 
unfit. Further, Workman admitted that he has no record and he remained absent from duty on the dates as 
mentioned in the charge sheet on his own. 


0. Thus, in view of the aforesaid statement of the CSE Workman and evidence recorded during the enquiry 
proceeding, the charge against the CSE Workman was found established under Standing Order No.25.25 for 
habitual absenteeism from the duty. Further, record reveals that show cause notice was served upon the CSE 
Workman for submitting his representation against the finding contained in the enquiry report and that got received 
by the Workman as _ per acknowledgement. Thereafter Disciplinary Authority after considering all the evidence 
and extenuating factors, passed the dismissal order dated 9.5.2008, finding the charge against workman grave and 
serious. Therefore, there is no illegality or impropriety or infirmity in the dismissal order of the Petitioner, passed 
by Respondent management. 


ll. Although Workman has taken plea that he remained absent during the year 2007 due to the reason that he 
was suffering from ill-health and also his uncle passed away and he could not be regular on duty. But Petitioner 
failed to produce any documents to substantiate his plea of illness. Therefore, for the want of any documentary 
evidence i.e., prescriptions of medical practitioner about his treatment of illness or medical certificate of unfit from 
competent medical practitioner. This plea of workman is not tenable. Further, workman failed to explain that 
why he could not report to the Company’s hospital about his sickness or report about his absenteeism to the 
Respondent. Therefore, for the want of above stated documentary evidence, the plea of illness taken by the 
Workman is nothing but ruse and feeble ground and same is not tenable. 


In this context, Hon’ble Supreme Court in Delhi Transport Corporation vs Sardar Singh 2004 SC 574 have 
held, that an employee absents himself from the duty even without sanctioned leave for a very long period, prima 
facie shows lack of interest in the work and the authority can on the basis of record come to the conclusion about 
employee being habitual negligent in duties and exhibited the lack of interest in the employers work, the burden is 
on employee who claimed that there is no negligence and lack of interest to establish it by placing the relevant 
material. But in the present case Petitioner utterly failed to produce any material in evidence to substantiate his 
plea of illness hence, he has rightly been held guilty of committing misconduct under Company’s Standing Order 
No.25.25 for habitual absenteeism from duty. 


Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court in its number of decisions have held that workman remaining absent from duty 
for a long time is a grave misconduct , few decisions of Hon’ble Courts are discussed hereunder: - 


In State of U.P. V. Ashok Kumar Singh 996 () SCC 302, wherein the Apex Court had held: - 


“Having notices the fact that the first Respondent has absented himself from duty without level on several 
occasions, we are unable to appreciate the High Court's observation that ‘his absence from duty would not amount 
to such a grave charge. Even otherwise on the facts of this case, there was no justification for the High Court to 
interfere with the punishment holding that 'the punishment does not commensurate with the gravity of the charge’ 
especially when the High Court concurred with the findings of the Tribunal on facts. No case for interference with 
the punishment is made out.” 


In the case of North Eastern Karnataka R.T. Corpn. v. Ashappa decided on 2 May, 2006 wherein, the Apex 
Court had held:- 


“Remaining absent for a long time, in our opinion, cannot be said to be a minor misconduct. The Appellant runs a 
fleet of buses. It is a statutory organization. It has to provide public utility services. For running the buses, the 
service of the conductor is imperative. No employer running a fleet of buses can allow an employee to remain 
absent for a long time. The Respondent had been given opportunities to resume his duties. Despite such notices, 
he remained absent. He was found not only to have remained absent for a period of more than three years, his 


[भाग वा--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त 6, 2025/श्रावण 25, 947 5683 


leave records were seen and it was found that he remained unauthorisedly absent on several occasions. In this 
view of the matter, it cannot be said that the misconduct committed by the Respondent herein has to be treated 
lightly. 

In Delhi Transport Corporation v. Sardar Singh [(2004) 7 SCC 574], the Apex Court held-: 


"II. Conclusions regarding negligence and lack of interest can be arrived at by looking into the period of 
absence, more particularly, when same is unauthorised. Burden is on the employee who claims that there was no 
negligence and/or lack of interest to establish it by placing relevant materials. Clause (ii) of para 4 of the Standing 
Orders shows the seriousness attached to habitual absence. In clause (i) thereof, there is requirement of prior 
permission. Only exception made is in case of sudden illness. There also conditions are stipulated, non-observance 
of which renders the absence unauthorised." 

State of U.P. v. Sheo Shanker Lal Srivastava and Others [(2006) 3 SCC 276], 
it was opined that, “the Industrial Courts or the High Courts would not normally interfere with the quantum 
of punishment imposed upon by the Respondent stating: "It is now well-settled that principles of law that the 
High Court or the Tribunal in exercise of its power of judicial review would not normally interfere with the 
quantum of punishment. Doctrine of proportionality can be invoked only under certain situations. It is now 
well-settled that the High Court shall be very slow in interfering with the quantum of punishment unless it is 
found to be shocking to one's conscience." 
The Hon’ble Apex Court in the case of Management Coal India Ltd. v. Mukul Kumar Choudhary Civil 
Appeal 5762-5763 of 2009 decided on 24.08.2009 laid down the test of proportionality of punishment and 
held:- 
“One of the test to be applied while dealing with the question of punishment would be: would any 
reasonable employer have imposed such punishment in like circumstances? Obviously, a reasonable 
employer is expected to take into consideration measure, magnitude and degree of misconduct and all other 
relevant circumstances and exclude irrelevant matters before imposing punishment.” 

In the case of Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation Vs. Dilip Uttam Jayabhay, the 2022 LLR 
page 26, wherein the Hon’ble Apex Court held:- 

“once the enquiry finding is held to be fair and proper, industrial Tribunal or Labour Court lacks jurisdiction to 
interfere with the quantum of punishment unless the same is shockingly disproportionate to the gravity of 
conduct.” 

Thus, in view of the fore gone discussion, I am of the considered view that the termination order of the Workman 
from service passed by the Respondent management is legal and justified and said dismissal order of Petitioner is 
liable to be confirmed. 

This issue is decided against the workman and in favour of the Respondent. 


2. Issue No.IV:- In view of the finding given in Issues No. I, I, HI & IV, the Petitioner is not entitled to

AWARD 


In view of the fore gone discussion and law laid down by the Hon'ble Apex Court as discussed above, the 
action of the General Manager, M/s. Singareni Collieries Company Ltd., Bellampalli Area, Goleti Township 
(P.O.), Adilabad Distt., in terminating the services of Sri Jellala Balaiah, Ex-Badli Filler, Goleti-! Inc, SCCo. Ltd., 
Bellampalli Area with effect from 9.5.2008 is held legal and justified. The workman is not entitled to any relief 
as prayed for. Reference is answered accordingly.

0. Here, on the point of territorial jurisdiction of this Tribunal, it is settled Law that as per the Division Bench

4. Here, the contention of the Petitioner/Workman is that he was re-appointed in the year 20I4 and he served the 
company for (5) years and he hails from a very poor family, he has got no other livelihood and facing untold 
financial problems and prayed to consider the case U/Sec.l-A of ID. Act. The ill-health suffered by the petitioner

5. Here, this Tribunal relied on a Division Bench Judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court rendered in Civil 
Appeal No.257/l999, dt.08.04.999 between Ajaib Singh vs. Sirhind Co-op. Marketing-cum-Processing Service 
Society Ltd., & another, wherein their lordships held that: - 


“The object of Industrial Disputes Act was to give succor to weaker sections of the society. The emergence of 
State implies an end to exploitation of workman and as a corollary to that collective bargaining came into it ow 
intended to protect workmen against victimization and exploitation by the employer and to ensure termination of 
peaceful manner. 


“The object of the Act, therefore, is to give succor to weaker sections of the society which is a pre-requisit 
ensure industrial peace and pre-empt industrial tension, the Act further aims at enhancing the industrial productior. 
to be life-blood of a developing society. The Act provides a machinery for investigation and settlement of industr 
legal technicalities with a view to avoid delays, by specially authorized Courts which are not supposed to deny the 
procedural wrangles”. 


5(a). Further, in a decision of the Hon’ble High Court reported in 20l2 (l) ALD 220 (DB), wherein their 
lordships observed that: - 


“The Industrial Disputes Act, /947 is a social welfare legislation, which required to be interpreted 
keeping in view the goals set out in the Preamble and Directive principles of State Policy in Part-IV of the 
Constitution. The Labour Court/Industrial Tribunal is conferred with very wide discretion 9/3$९८/।-4 of the 
Act for granting appropriate relief”’. 


6. Here, their Lordships of the Hon’ble Gujarat High Court in a case rendered on 04.05.994, Between: 
Management of Glaxo India Ltd., Vs. State of Assam and 3 others categorically observed that “a Labour Court is 
required to settle a dispute according to the principles of natural justice, equity and good conscience and law 
without attaching undue importance to legal technicalities”. 


7. Here, it is to be noted that the concept of Industrial Dispute is quite broad and with the passage of time its 
horizon is being expanded. Further, the disputes are required to be resolved for the purpose of establishing peaceful 
and cordial atmosphere in an industry. Peace and harmony are the quintessential aspects which are to be kept in 
view while dealing with the “/is” or “controversy” relating to any industry. Apart from the above, whether the 
impugned punishment is so disproportionate as to shock the conscience of the Court, has to be decided on the facts 
of each case, having due regard to the gravity of misconduct & nature of duties discharged by the delinquent 
employee. 


8. Further, the Hon’ble Madras High Court observed in a case rendered in Management of Hyudai Motor India 
Ltd Vs. T.Sudhakar ... on 377 January, 2022: 


5690 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA AUGUST 6, 2025/SHRAVANA 25, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


“When scales of justice stands balanced in a given case, the tilt to be exercised should be in favour of 
the poor workmen rather than the mighty Managements.” 


9. Therefore, in view of the above mitigating circumstances of the case, this Tribunal is of the opinion that the 
extreme punishment of dismissal from service imposed by the respondents/company against the 
petitioner/workman is harsh, disproportionate and shocks to conscience of this Tribunal, hence, deserves to be 
modified since the disciplinary authority cannot be permitted to act arbitrarily and work like a Roman Knight and 
it cannot be allowed a fight between David and Goliath as in the present case on hand. Moreover, the facts of this 
case attracts the proverbial saying “Every saint has a past and every sinner has a future”. Moreover, facts of this 
case attracts the proverbial saying “Every saint has a past and every sinner has a future” and Biblical proverbs 
“Speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves, for the rights of all who are destitute” and “Speak up and 
judge fairly; defend the rights of the poor and needy.” Further, “Heavens would not have fallen if one more 
opportunity is given for the petitioner”. 


20. This Tribunal has perused, analyzed and meditated upon the case at hand, the case laws and principles of law 
referred above. In view of the above facts and circumstances and keeping in view of the principle “temper justice 
with mercy” and to meet the ends of justice, this Tribunal is of the opinion that the punishment of removal from 
service imposed on the petitioner is disproportionate and shocks the conscience of this Tribunal and hence, it 
deserves to be modified appropriately. Taking a holistic view of the matter, this Tribunal is of considered view that 
the extreme punishment of dismissal from service imposed on the petitioner deserves to be modified. However, 
since the charges leveled against the petitioner are proved, the relief is to be molded by this Tribunal appropriately 
and this Tribunal is of the considered opinion that the petitioner is entitled to be reinstated into service as “Afresh 
Badli Filler” only. Consequently, the petitioner is not entitled to any back wages, any continuity of service and 
any attendant benefits, since petitioner might have gainfully employed during pendency of this Industrial Dispute. 
Hence, the punishment of dismissal from service imposed by the Respondents Company is hereby modified 
appropriately. Accordingly, the Point No.2 & 3 are answered. 


2. IN THE RESULT, the petition is partly allowed. The dismissal order dt.25.0!.202] under Ex.M- passed by 
the Respondent No.2 is hereby modified. The respondents’/company is directed to reinstate the petitioner into 
service as “Afresh Badli Filler” only, but without any continuity of service, without any attendant benefits and 
without any back wages. The petitioner is entitled to the salary only from the date of publication this Award. Copy 
of the Award be sent to the appropriate Government for publication. Both parties shall bear their own costs.

l. This is a Petition filed under Section 2A of the ID act. The claim set forth by the [7 party workman is that 


she was appointed as an Assistant by the 2" Party in a clear vacancy of Office Assistant w.e.f. 02.08.200 by 
obtaining an Application and she has attended the interview conducted by the II Party; she was also assured with 


[भाग व--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त 6, 2025/श्रावण 25, 947 5693 


regularization of her services for the services rendered by her and that she was doing the duties of regular staff; 
that she was not paid with minimum scales as applicable to the Assistants and took work for more than eight hours 
per day without paying her overtime wages; inspite of repeated requests to absorb her to the permanent post she 
was deprived with the benefits of the permanent employees; that she was not provided with Provident Fund, Bonus 
Benefits though other employees were extended with the same; that she was suddenly retrenched from the services 
of the II Party orally from 6.2.20l7 in the morning hours by the Branch Manager without notice, without 
payment of notice pay / retrenchment compensation though there were no allegations against her. She was 
retrenched from the services without prior intimation or paying her retrenchment compensation and without 
following due process of law and that the II Party has retrenched more than 20 workmen without filing approval 
application seeking permission from the appropriate Government to retrench their services as mandated under 
Section 25N of the Act; that due to the retrenchment she is facing irreparable hardship, agony and unable to run 
her family and that she does not know any other work than the Assistant job; that the II Party has employed fresh 
entrants in her place and the nature of work done by her is perennial in nature and taking the new entrants is illegal 
and malafide; that she raised an industrial dispute since no settlement was arrived she preferred to file the present 
petition requesting this Tribunal to declare the retrenchment of service by the II Party as not in accordance with the 
provisions of ID Act; reinstate her into service with full backwages and other benefits, regularization with 
continuity of service and ancillary benefits from the date of her appointment 02.08.200 with cost. 


23 The 2™ Party in their Counter Statement rebutted the Claim Statement stating that all the averments made 
are false; that LIC of India (Staff) Regulations, 960 are not applicable to the temporary employees appointed by 
the II Party; that the I Party is put to strict proof of the above averments; that she was doing some unspecified job 
on daily wages on need basis and that they were paying wages as per the notification issued by the Government of 
Karnataka from time to time and therefore the question of extending Provident Fund Benefits does not arise. As 
the specified job was completed, her services were disengaged as per law and the question of issuing notice, 
retrenchment compensation or notice pay does not arise and that the II Party has not contravened the provisions of 
ID Act and the question of reinstatement with the back wages and other benefits does not arise. The Respondent 
has prayed for dismissal of the Petition with cost. 


3. On the rival pleadings the following points arise for consideration: 


“0l. Whether the I Party has succeeded in proving that she was appointed by the I Party as 
Assistant on temporary basis in a clear vacancy as contended? 


02. Whether the disengagement of the I Party from job by the II Party is illegal as contended 
by the I Party? 


03. Whether the I Party is entitled for the reliefs prayed for? 
04. What is the proper order to be passed?” 


4. The I party has got examined herself as WW | and Ex W-! to Ex W-I] are got marked. From the side of 
the II Party MW | is examined and Ex M-] is marked. 

5. Heard the arguments advanced by both sides. Written notes of Arguments are also submitted by both 
sides. 

6. POINTS NO. TO 3: Since the matter to be considered and adjudicated on these points are intertwined 


and interwoven, all these points are discussed together. 


7. The I Party WW | claimed herself as a temporary employee / Assistant in Class III Category in a clear 
vacancy of Office Assistant under the II Party LIC of India since 02.08.200 at its Harihara Branch and continued 
to work for seven years till 6.2.207. Her case is that she has put in an application before the II Party and she 
was interviewed by the officials of the LIC at the Branch Office. According to her she was appointed with an 
assurance of regularization of her service within a few years coupled with the benefits applicable to permanent 
Assistants. The above claim of the I Party is stoutly denied by the II Party on the precincts that the I Party was 
engaged by the LIC purely on daily wages to perform some unspecified jobs and she has been paid daily wage for 
the days of her engagement. Such payment according to the II Party has never been meant as “SALARY”. 


8. Among the documents produced and proved by WW l, there is nothing indicting her to have been called 
for an interview for the post of Office Assistant. She did not produce copy of application said to have been 
submitted by her before the II Party to the said post. Though she claimed that the II Party did publish notification 
calling for applications on their notice board, she could not specify the date of notification or its exhibition on the 
notice board. She was not issued with any appointment letter by the II Party. On meticulous cross-examination she 
testified that she was appointed on temporary basis as daily wager. She was given wages for the period she served 
in the II Party. Ex W-I series are the five vouchers produced by the I Party to prove the payments received by her 
from the II Party LIC. The vouchers reflect the wages received by the I Party and similarly placed other workers. 
Those vouchers would never improve her case, much less it substantiates her contention that she was appointed in 


5694 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA AUGUST 6, 2025/SHRAVANA 25, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


a clear vacancy by undergoing regular recruitment process. Those vouchers would never indicate continuous and 
uninterrupted service of the I Party under the II Party for seven years as contended by her. 


9. MW | the Divisional Manager of the II Party specifically deposed that there is no particular notification 
for LIC separately for daily wage employees and such daily wagers were engaged based on need and requirements 
and there is no prescribed recruitment procedure for engaging them. Their wages were paid monthly in cash, 
debited from imprest Cash Account No. l772. This fact stood revealed from Ex ४४-] series vouchers. MW | 
reiterated that no order is issued to such persons for engaging them on daily wage. So without getting an 
appointment order from the management the I Party worker cannot qualify herself to be entitled for permanency or 
rather regularization in the job. There is no basis for the so called assurance alleged to have been given by the II 
Party that she would be given permanency in service along with equivalent other benefits. 


0. The purpose of production of Ex W-2 by the I Party, the confidential communication issued by the 
Regional Manager (P&IR) to all SDM under South Central Zones dated 25..20I7 alerting the divisions to 
disengage all the daily wagers who are continued without any court case and calling for the number of daily 
wagers continuing by virtue of court cases pursuant to the decision of the competent authority is not profitably 
explained by the I Party. It is also not properly explained as to how the I Party / WW | happened to be in custody 
of Ex W-2, the confidential communication addressed to the SDM by its higher-up. Anyhow Ex ४४-२2 is not of any 
help to the I Party to establish her case. 


Il. Ex W-3 dated 25.2.20l7 is the representation made by the I Party to the Senior Divisional Manager 
seeking regularization of her service being aggrieved by stoppage of her service w.e.f. 6.2.207 stating the same 
as retrenchment. In Ex W-3 she grieved before the authority that she was pulled out from job without notice and 
without payment of notice pay / retrenchment compensation despite having no allegations against her. 


2. On 27.2.20I7 she took up the matter for conciliation before the Assistant Labour Commissioner (C), 
Hubli under Ex W-4. Ex W-5 is the reply submitted by the II Party before the ALC(C), Hubli, in response to the 
Ex W-4 representation. All along, the II Party has adopted a firm defence that the I Party was engaged only as a 
daily wager on need basis due to office exigencies and she was neither recruited not given any appointment letter 
by any authority. Her engagement was purely on daily wages for carrying out work on piece meal basis depending 
upon the needs of the office and not as a temporary employee. Her payment of wages was as per the Government 
of Karnataka Gazette Notification revised from time to time. MW |] during her evidence precisely testified that 
since the I Party was paid wages counting the number of days she worked, no deduction was made from her wage 
towards Provident Fund and payment of bonus to her also did not arise for consideration. The circumstances 
explained by MW | substantiates the contention raised by the II Party that the I Party was engaged only as a daily 
wager without there being any assurance of permanency of service and such alleged assurance being out of place. 


3. Ex W-6 is the application filed by the I Party before the ALC(C) calling for documents from the II party 
during the conciliation proceedings. As per Ex W-7 the Assistant Labour Commissioner(C) conducted Joint 
Discussion on 05.02.208 notifying further joint discussion to another date. Ex W-8 is also a similar application 
filed by the I Party before the Conciliation Officer calling for some more documents from the II party during the 
conciliation proceedings. Ex W-9 is the letter issued by the ALC(C) to LEO for collection of photocopies of 
documents from various branches. Ex W-I0 is the copy of notification to the post of Recruitment of Assistant 
published by the II Party on !7.09.209. She did not prefer to put in an Application against such notification. She 
testified that she is not eligible to file application to the said post. Ex W-] is the representation given by the I 
Party to the Chairman, LIC of India requesting to appoint her to the vacancy notified and if not, to keep vacant one 
post of Office Assistant till the instant case gets over. 


4. None of the above documents produced and relied upon by the I Party renders any proof to the core point 
of controversy as to the status of employment at the time of her engagement under the II Party. Indeed, had it been 
an engagement as Daily Wager, she does not get entitled for any of the benefits sought in the Petition. The II Party 
Management to buttress its contention that the I Party was simply disengaged as there existed no further 
requirement of her service and she has not been a temporary employee capable of claiming any of the benefits 
sought for, relied upon various judicial pronouncements of the Hon’ble Apex Court. At the threshold it has to be 
observed that the I Party failed in showing any Rule, Law or Regulation nor any administrative order on the basis 
of which she claims reinstatement and regularization with continuity of Service and other monetory benefits. In 
order to high light the said aspect the I Party has relied upon the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Subedar Singh and 
others vs. District Judge, Mirzapur and another 200 SCC 37. 


5. It is contextually significant to follow the dictum laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of 
Haryana vs. Jasmer Singh (996 (Il) SCC 77) which reads : 


“The respondents, therefore in the present appeals who are employed on daily wages cannot be 
treated as on a par with persons in regular service of the State of Haryana holding similar posts. 
Daily-rated workers are not required to possess the qualifications prescribed for regular workers, 
nor do they have to fulfil the requirement relating to age at the time of recruitment. They are not 
selected in the manner in which regular employees are selected. In other words the requirements for 


[भाग वा--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त 6, 2025/श्रावण 25, 947 5695 


selection are not as rigorous. There are also other provisions relating to regular service such as the 
liability of a member of the service to be transferred, and his being subject to the disciplinary 
jurisdiction of the authorities as prescribed, which the daily-rated workmen are not subjected to. 
They cannot, therefore, be equated with regular workmen for the purposes for their wages. Nor can 
they claim the minimum of the regular pay-scale of the regularly employed” 


Referring to the said legal position the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Haryana and another vs. Tilak Raj and 
others (2003 (6) SCC 23) held that a scale of pay is attached to a definite post and in case of a daily wager, he 
holds no posts. The I Party neither in her pleadings nor in evidence has made out the particular works she 
performed under the II Party, much less any material is placed by her as to the nature of the duties for which she 
was engaged by the II Party. The contention of the I Party in its Statement of Objection that the engagement of the 
I Party was for meeting the office exigencies to attend some unspecified jobs on payment of daily wage for the 
work performed is thus well founded. 


6. In Mohammed Ashif and others vs. State of Bihar and others (200 (5) SCC 475), the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court held that the question of regularization of services of an Employee may arise only in situations where against 
an available clear vacancy an appointment is made on adhoc or on-daily wage basis by an authority competent to 
do so without any artificial break in service. The second situation in which the regularization could be granted is 
held to be where the initial entry of the employee against an available vacancy was found suffering from some 
flaws in the procedure in making the appointment though the person appointing was competent to make such initial 
recruitment and had otherwise followed the procedure prescribed for such recruitment. It is equally held that “the 
all-important condition precedent for such regularization is that the initial entry of such employee must be made 
against the Sanctioned vacancy and by following the Rules and Regulations governing such entry”. 


7. Similarly the constitution bench of the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Karnataka vs. Uma Devi (2006 
(4) SCC ) held that “Jf it is a contractual appointment, the appointment comes to an end at the end of the 
contract, if it were an engagement or appointment on daily wages or casual basis, the same would come to an end 
when it is discontinued. Similarly, a temporary employee could not claim to be made permanent on the expiry of 
his term of appointment. It has also to be clarified that merely because a temporary employee or a casual wage 
worker is continued for a time beyond the term of his appointment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed in 
regular service or made permanent, merely on the strength of such continuance, if the original appointment was 
not made by following a due process of selection as envisaged by the relevant rules. It is not open to the court to 
prevent regular recruitment at the instance of temporary employees whose period of employment has come to an 
end or of ad hoc employees who by the very nature of their appointment, do not acquire any right.” Here in the 
instant case the I party is claiming permanency and seeks for regularization mainly on the so called “Jong duration 
of work” (emphasis supplied) and not on any other valid ground. The dictum quoted above defeats her claim as it 
is bereft of valid support and devoid of merit. 


8. Most of the rulings placed by the I party are not applicable to the facts of the case on hand. The Verdict of 
the Hon’ble High Court of Madras in V Muthukumarasamy and others vs. The Chairman, LIC, Zonal Office 
dated 2.0.2007 also does not get any application in view of the fact involved in that case as the Petitioners 
therein were sponsored by the Employment Exchange and have been appointed on temporary basis from 
shortlisted candidates. As already observed, the I Party herein was not sponsored by Employment Exchange nor 
her engagement was in a clear vacancy by undergoing the Regular Recruitment process. 


9. The I party further relied upon on the ruling of the Hon’ble High Court of Karnataka, Bengaluru in R V 
Mohan Reddy vs. The Chairman, Karnataka Grameena Bank in WP No. 944/2022 (L-RES) dated 
0.02.2025 awarding 60% of Backwages to the Employee from the date of his termination reckoning the two 
decades of service he had under the management as a Peon on daily wage. As against that, the principle laid down 
by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in a plethora of rulings aforementioned consistently hold that the Casual 
Employment terminates when the same is discontinued, and merely because a temporary or casual worker has been 
engaged beyond the period of his employment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed into regular service or 
made permanent, if the original appointment was not in terms of the process envisaged by the relevant rules. So 
the legal position settled at rest by the Hon’ble Supreme Court disentitles the I party to put forth any claim of 
reinstatement, regularization, continuity of service or back wages with consequential benefits. 


20. To sum up, the solitary materials viz., Ex W-l vouchers show only pay for a single month in the 
respective years and there is no valid material proving that her engagement was continuous in nature and she 
performed duties under the II Party continuously till the date of her disengagement so as to show that her tenure of 
service at a time was more than 240 days in a calendar year and her disengagement was in violation of the 
provisions of Section 25F of the ID Act. So on legal principle and on factual matrix the I Party failed to establish a 
case on merit justifying the relief sought for in the instant Industrial Dispute. Eventually her Claim Petition fails 
and the same is liable to be dismissed. With this view Points No. | to 3 are answered accordingly. 


2I. POINT NO. 4: In view of the above discussion, the I party is held as not entitled for any relief. 


5696 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA AUGUST 6, 2025/SHRAVANA 25, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)]

I5. It is contextually significant to follow the dictum laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of 
Haryana vs. Jasmer Singh (996 (l) SCC 77) which reads : 


“The respondents, therefore in the present appeals who are employed on daily wages cannot be 
treated as on a par with persons in regular service of the State of Haryana holding similar posts. 
Daily-rated workers are not required to possess the qualifications prescribed for regular workers, 
nor do they have to fulfil the requirement relating to age at the time of recruitment. They are not

selected in the manner in which regular employees are selected. In other words the requirements for 
selection are not as rigorous. There are also other provisions relating to regular service such as the 
liability of a member of the service to be transferred, and his being subject to the disciplinary 
jurisdiction of the authorities as prescribed, which the daily-rated workmen are not subjected to. 
They cannot, therefore, be equated with regular workmen for the purposes for their wages. Nor can 
they claim the minimum of the regular pay-scale of the regularly employed” 


Referring to the said legal position the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Haryana and another vs. Tilak Raj and 
others (2003 (6) SCC 23) held that a scale of pay is attached to a definite post and in case of a daily wager, he 
holds no posts. The I Party neither in his pleadings nor in evidence has made out the particular works he 
performed under the II Party, much less any material is placed by him as to the nature of the duties for which he 
was engaged by the II Party. The contention of the II Party in its Statement of Objection that the engagement of the 
I Party was for meeting the office exigencies to attend some unspecified jobs on payment of daily wage for the 
work performed is thus well founded. 


6. In Mohammed Ashif and others vs. State of Bihar and others (200 (5) SCC 475), the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court held that the question of regularization of services of an Employee may arise only in situations where against 
an available clear vacancy an appointment is made on adhoc or on-daily wage basis by an authority competent to 
do so without any artificial break in service. The second situation in which the regularization could be granted is 
held to be where the initial entry of the employee against an available vacancy was found suffering from some 
flaws in the procedure in making the appointment though the person appointing was competent to make such initial 
recruitment and had otherwise followed the procedure prescribed for such recruitment. It is equally held that “the 
all-important condition precedent for such regularization is that the initial entry of such employee must be made 
against the Sanctioned vacancy and by following the Rules and Regulations governing such entry”. 


7. Similarly the constitution bench of the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Karnataka vs. Uma Devi (2006 
(4) SCC ) held that “Jf it is a contractual appointment, the appointment comes to an end at the end of the 
contract, if it were an engagement or appointment on daily wages or casual basis, the same would come to an end 
when it is discontinued. Similarly, a temporary employee could not claim to be made permanent on the expiry of 
his term of appointment. It has also to be clarified that merely because a temporary employee or a casual wage 
worker is continued for a time beyond the term of his appointment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed in 
regular service or made permanent, merely on the strength of such continuance, if the original appointment was 
not made by following a due process of selection as envisaged by the relevant rules. It is not open to the court to 
prevent regular recruitment at the instance of temporary employees whose period of employment has come to an 
end or of ad hoc employees who by the very nature of their appointment, do not acquire any right.” Here in the 
instant case the I party is claiming permanency and seeks for regularization mainly on the so called “Jong duration 
of work” (emphasis supplied) and not on any other valid ground. The dictum quoted above defeats his claim as it is 
bereft of valid support and devoid of merit. 


8. Most of the rulings placed by the I party are not applicable to the facts of the case on hand. The Verdict of 
the Hon’ble High Court of Madras in V Muthukumarasamy and others vs. The Chairman, LIC, Zonal Office 
dated 2.0.2007 also does not get any application in view of the fact involved in that case as the Petitioners 
therein were sponsored by the Employment Exchange and have been appointed on temporary basis from 
shortlisted candidates. As already observed, the I Party herein was not sponsored by Employment Exchange nor 
her engagement was in a clear vacancy by undergoing the Regular Recruitment process. 


9. The I party further relied upon on the ruling of the Hon’ble High Court of Karnataka, Bengaluru in R V 
Mohan Reddy vs. The Chairman, Karnataka Grameena Bank in WP No. 944/2022 (L-RES) dated 
0.02.2025 awarding 60% of Backwages to the Employee from the date of his termination reckoning the two 
decades of service he had under the management as a Peon on daily wage. As against that, the principle laid down 
by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in a plethora of rulings aforementioned consistently hold that the Casual 
Employment terminates when the same is discontinued, and merely because a temporary or casual worker has been 
engaged beyond the period of his employment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed into regular service or 
made permanent, if the original appointment was not in terms of the process envisaged by the relevant rules. So 
the legal position settled at rest by the Hon’ble Supreme Court disentitles the I party to put forth any claim of 
reinstatement, regularization, continuity of service or back wages with consequential benefits. 


20. To sum up, the solitary materials viz., Ex W-I seires indicate the payment made to the I Party in the year 
205 alone for the month of March and November and there is no valid material proving that his engagement was 
continuous in nature and hhe performed duties under the II Party continuously till the date of his disengagement so 
as to show that his tenure of service at a time was more than 240 days in a calendar year and his disengagement

Party failed to establish a case on merit justifying the relief sought for in the instant Industrial Dispute. Eventually 
his Claim Petition fails and the same is liable to be dismissed. With this view Points No. | to 3 are answered 
accordingly.

requirement of her service and she has not been a temporary employee capable of claiming any of the benefits 
sought for, relied upon various judicial pronouncements of the Hon’ble Apex Court. At the threshold it has to be 
observed that the I Party failed in showing any Rule, Law or Regulation nor any administrative order on the basis 
of which she claims reinstatement and regularization with continuity of Service and other monetory benefits. In 
order to high light the said aspect the II Party has relied upon the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Subedar Singh and 
others vs. District Judge, Mirzapur and another 200l SCC 37.

5. It is contextually significant to follow the dictum laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of 
Haryana vs. Jasmer Singh (996 (l) SCC 77) which reads : 


“The respondents, therefore in the present appeals who are employed on daily wages cannot be 
treated as on a par with persons in regular service of the State of Haryana holding similar posts. 
Daily-rated workers are not required to possess the qualifications prescribed for regular workers, 
nor do they have to fulfil the requirement relating to age at the time of recruitment. They are not 
selected in the manner in which regular employees are selected. In other words the requirements for 
selection are not as rigorous. There are also other provisions relating to regular service such as the 
liability of a member of the service to be transferred, and his being subject to the disciplinary 
jurisdiction of the authorities as prescribed, which the daily-rated workmen are not subjected to. 
They cannot, therefore, be equated with regular workmen for the purposes for their wages. Nor can 
they claim the minimum of the regular pay-scale of the regularly employed” 


Referring to the said legal position the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Haryana and another vs. Tilak Raj and 
others (2003 (6) SCC 23) held that a scale of pay is attached to a definite post and in case of a daily wager, he 
holds no posts. The I Party neither in her pleadings nor in evidence has made out the particular works she 
performed under the II Party, much less any material is placed by her as to the nature of the duties for which she 
was engaged by the II Party. The contention of the I Party in its Statement of Objection that the engagement of the 
I Party was for meeting the office exigencies to attend some unspecified jobs on payment of daily wage for the 
work performed is thus well founded. 


6. In Mohammed Ashif and others vs. State of Bihar and others (200 (5) SCC 475), the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court held that the question of regularization of services of an Employee may arise only in situations where against 
an available clear vacancy an appointment is made on adhoc or on-daily wage basis by an authority competent to 
do so without any artificial break in service. The second situation in which the regularization could be granted is 
held to be where the initial entry of the employee against an available vacancy was found suffering from some 
flaws in the procedure in making the appointment though the person appointing was competent to make such initial 
recruitment and had otherwise followed the procedure prescribed for such recruitment. It is equally held that “the 
all-important condition precedent for such regularization is that the initial entry of such employee must be made 
against the Sanctioned vacancy and by following the Rules and Regulations governing such entry”. 


7. Similarly the constitution bench of the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Karnataka vs. Uma Devi (2006 
(4) SCC ) held that “Jf it is a contractual appointment, the appointment comes to an end at the end of the 
contract, if it were an engagement or appointment on daily wages or casual basis, the same would come to an end 
when it is discontinued. Similarly, a temporary employee could not claim to be made permanent on the expiry of 
his term of appointment. It has also to be clarified that merely because a temporary employee or a casual wage 
worker is continued for a time beyond the term of his appointment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed in 
regular service or made permanent, merely on the strength of such continuance, if the original appointment was 
not made by following a due process of selection as envisaged by the relevant rules. It is not open to the court to 
prevent regular recruitment at the instance of temporary employees whose period of employment has come to an 
end or of ad hoc employees who by the very nature of their appointment, do not acquire any right.” Here in the 
instant case the I party is claiming permanency and seeks for regularization mainly on the so called “Jong duration 
of work” (emphasis supplied) and not on any other valid ground. The dictum quoted above defeats her claim as it 
is bereft of valid support and devoid of merit. 


8. Most of the rulings placed by the I party are not applicable to the facts of the case on hand. The Verdict of 
the Hon’ble High Court of Madras in V Muthukumarasamy and others vs. The Chairman, LIC, Zonal Office 
dated 2.0.2007 also does not get any application in view of the fact involved in that case as the Petitioners 
therein were sponsored by the Employment Exchange and have been appointed on temporary basis from 
shortlisted candidates. As already observed, the I Party herein was not sponsored by Employment Exchange nor 
her engagement was in a clear vacancy by undergoing the Regular Recruitment process.

Mohan Reddy vs. The Chairman, Karnataka Grameena Bank in WP No. 944/2022 (L-RES) dated 
0.02.2025 awarding 60% of Backwages to the Employee from the date of his termination reckoning the two 
decades of service he had under the management as a Peon on daily wage. As against that, the principle laid down 
by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in a plethora of rulings aforementioned consistently hold that the Casual 
Employment terminates when the same is discontinued, and merely because a temporary or casual worker has been 
engaged beyond the period of his employment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed into regular service or 
made permanent, if the original appointment was not in terms of the process envisaged by the relevant rules. So 
the legal position settled at rest by the Hon’ble Supreme Court disentitles the I party to put forth any claim of 
reinstatement, regularization, continuity of service or back wages with consequential benefits.

service at a time was more than 240 days in a calendar year and her disengagement was in violation of the

l. This is a Petition filed under Section 2A of the ID act. The claim set forth by the |“ party workman is that 


she was appointed as an Assistant by the 2" Party in a clear vacancy of Office Assistant w.e.f. 03.05.20I5 by

that she was not paid with minimum scales as applicable to the Assistants and took work for more than eight hours 
per day without paying her overtime wages; inspite of repeated requests to absorb her to the permanent post she 
was deprived with the benefits of the permanent employees; that she was not provided with Provident Fund, Bonus 
Benefits though other employees were extended with the same; that she was suddenly retrenched from the services 
of the II Party orally from 02.07.20l6 in the morning hours by the Branch Manager without notice, without 
payment of notice pay / retrenchment compensation though there were no allegations against her. She was 
retrenched from the services without prior intimation or paying her retrenchment compensation and without 
following due process of law. As per Section 25N of the ID Act, the II Party should have filed application seeking 
permission from the appropriate Government to retrench her services with copy to her; that due to the 
retrenchment she is facing irreparable hardship, agony and unable to run her family and that she does not know any 
other work than the Assistant job; that the II Party has employed fresh entrants in her place and the nature of work 
done by her is perennial in nature and taking the new entrants is illegal and malafide; that she raised an industrial 
dispute since no settlement was arrived she preferred to file the present petition requesting this Tribunal to declare 
the retrenchment of service by the II Party as not in accordance with the provisions of ID Act; reinstate her into 
service with full back wages and other benefits, regularization with continuity of service and ancillary benefits 
from the date of her appointment 03.05.205 with cost. 


2. The 2" Party in their Counter Statement rebutted the Claim Statement stating that all the averments made 
are false; that LIC of India (Staff) Regulations, 960 are not applicable to the temporary employees appointed by 
the II Party; that the I Party is put to strict proof of the above averments; that she was doing some unspecified job 
on daily wages on need basis and that they were paying wages as per the notification issued by the Government of 
Karnataka from time to time and therefore the question of extending Provident Fund Benefits does not arise. As 
the specified job was completed, her services were disengaged as per law and the question of issuing notice, 
retrenchment compensation or notice pay does not arise and that the II Party has not contravened the provisions of 
ID Act and the question of reinstatement with the backwages and other benefits does not arise. The Respondent 
has prayed for dismissal of the Petition with cost. 


3. On the rival pleadings the following points arise for consideration: 


“0i. Whether the I Party has succeeded in proving that she was appointed by the I Party as 
Assistant on temporary basis in a clear vacancy as contended? 


02. Whether the disengagement of the I Party from job by the II Party is illegal as contended 
by the I Party? 


03. Whether the I Party is entitled for the reliefs prayed for? 
04. What is the proper order to be passed?”

the II Party MW | is examined and Ex M-] is marked. 

Ds Heard the arguments advanced by both sides. Written notes of Arguments are also submitted by both 
sides. 

6. POINTS NO. TO 3: Since the matter to be considered and adjudicated on these points are intertwined 


and interwoven, all these points are discussed together. 


7. The I Party WW | claimed herself as a temporary employee / Assistant in Class III Category in a clear 
vacancy of Office Assistant under the II Party LIC of India since 03.05.20I5 at its Davanagere I Branch and 
continued to work for One year till 02.07.206. Her case is that she has put in an application before the II Party 


570 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA AUGUST 6, 2025/SHRAVANA 25, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


and she was interviewed by the officials of the LIC at the Branch Office. According to her she was appointed with 
an assurance of regularization of her service within a few years coupled with the benefits applicable to permanent 
Assistants. The above claim of the I Party is stoutly denied by the II Party on the precincts that the I Party was 
engaged by the LIC purely on daily wages to perform some unspecified jobs and she has been paid daily wage for 
the days of her engagement. Such payment according to the II Party has never been meant as “SALARY”. 


8. Among the documents produced and proved by WW l, there is nothing indicting her to have been called 
for an interview for the post of Office Assistant. She did not produce copy of application said to have been 
submitted by her before the II Party to the said post. Though she claimed that the II Party did publish notification 
calling for applications on their notice board, she could not specify the date of notification or its exhibition on the 
notice board. She was not issued with any appointment letter by the II Party. On meticulous cross-examination she 
testified that she was appointed on temporary basis as daily wager. She was given wages for the period she served 
in the II Party. Ex ४४-] series are the two vouchers produced by the I Party to prove the payments received by her 
from the II Party LIC. The vouchers reflect the wages received by the I Party and similarly placed other workers. 
Those vouchers would never improve her case, much less it substantiates her contention that she was appointed in 
a clear vacancy by undergoing regular recruitment process. Those vouchers would never indicate continuous and 
uninterrupted service of the I Party under the II Party for One year as contended by her. 


9. MW | the Divisional Manager of the II Party specifically deposed that there is no particular notification 
for LIC separately for daily wage employees and such daily wagers were engaged based on need and requirements 
and there is no prescribed recruitment procedure for engaging them. Their wages were paid monthly in cash, 
debited from imprest Cash Account No. l772. This fact stood revealed from Ex ५४-] series vouchers. MW | 
reiterated that no order is issued to such persons for engaging them on daily wage. So without getting an 
appointment order from the management the I Party worker cannot qualify for herself to be entitled for 
permanency or rather regularization in the job. There is no basis for the so called assurance alleged to have been 
given by the II Party that she would be given permanency in service along with equivalent other benefits. 


0. The purpose of production of Ex W-2 by the I Party, the confidential communication issued by the 
Regional Manager (P&IR) to all SDM under South Central Zones dated 25..207 alerting the divisions to 
disengage all the daily wagers who are continued without any court case and calling for the number of daily 
wagers continuing by virtue of court cases pursuant to the decision of the competent authority is not profitably 
explained by the I Party. It is also not properly explained as to how the I Party / WW | happened to be in custody 
of Ex W-2, the confidential communication addressed to the SDM by its higher-up. Anyhow Ex ४४-२2 is not of any 
help to the I Party to establish her case. 


Il. Ex W-3 dated 25.2.207 is the representation made by the I Party to the Senior Divisional Manager 
seeking regularization of her service being aggrieved by stoppage of her service w.e.f. 02.07.206 stating the same 
as retrenchment. In Ex W-3 she grieved before the authority that she was pulled out from job without notice and 
without payment of notice pay / retrenchment compensation despite having no allegations against her. 


2. On 25.2.20I7 she took up the matter for conciliation before the Assistant Labour Commissioner (C), 
Hubli under Ex W-4. Ex W-5 is the reply submitted by the II Party before the ALC(C), Hubli, in response to the 
Ex W-4 representation. All along, the II Party has adopted a firm defence that the I Party was engaged only as a 
daily wager on need basis due to office exigencies and she was neither recruited not given any appointment letter 
by any authority. Her engagement was purely on daily wages for carrying out work on peace meal basis 
depending upon the needs of the office and not as a temporary employee. Her pay of wages was as per the 
Government of Karnataka Gazette Notification revised from time to time. MW I during her evidence precisely 
testified that since the I Party was paid wages counting the number of days she worked, no deduction was made 
from her wage towards Provident Fund and payment of bonus to her also did not arise for consideration. The 
circumstances explained by MW | substantiates the contention raised by the II Party that the I Party was engaged 
only as a daily wager without there being any assurance of permanency of service and such alleged assurance 
being out of place. 


3. Ex W-6 is the application filed by the I Party before the ALC(C) calling for documents from the II party 
during the conciliation proceedings. As per Ex W-7 the Assistant Labour Commissioner(C) conducted Joint 
Discussion on 05.02.208 notifying further joint discussion to another date. Ex W-8 is also a similar application 
filed by the I Party before the Conciliation Officer calling for some more documents from the II party during the 
conciliation proceedings. Ex W-9 is the letter issued by the ALC(C) to LEO for collection of photocopies of 
documents from various branches. Ex W-I0 is the copy of notification to the post of Recruitment of Assistant 
published by the II Party on 7.09.209. She did not prefer to put in an Application against such notification. She 
testified that she is not eligible to file application to the said post. Ex W-l] is the representation given by the I 
Party to the Chairman, LIC of India requesting to appoint her to the vacancy notified and if not, to keep vacant one 
post of Office Assistant till the instant case gets over. 


4. None of the above documents produced and relied upon by the I Party renders any proof to the core point 
of controversy as to the status of employment at the time of her engagement under the II Party. Indeed, had it been

an engagement as Daily Wager, she does not get entitled for any of the benefits sought in the Petition. The II Party 
Management to buttress its contention that the I Party was simply disengaged as there existed no further 
requirement of her service and she has not been a temporary employee capable of claiming any of the benefits 
sought for, relied upon various judicial pronouncements of the Hon’ble Apex Court. At the threshold it has to be 
observed that the I Party failed in showing any Rule, Law or Regulation nor any administrative order on the basis 
of which she claims reinstatement and regularization with continuity of Service and other monetory benefits. In 
order to high light the said aspect the I] Party has relied upon the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Subedar Singh and 
others vs. District Judge, Mirzapur and another 200 SCC 37. 


5. It is contextually significant to follow the dictum laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of 
Haryana vs. Jasmer Singh (996 (l) SCC 77) which reads : 


“The respondents, therefore in the present appeals who are employed on daily wages cannot be 
treated as on a par with persons in regular service of the State of Haryana holding similar posts. 
Daily-rated workers are not required to possess the qualifications prescribed for regular workers, 
nor do they have to fulfil the requirement relating to age at the time of recruitment. They are not 
selected in the manner in which regular employees are selected. In other words the requirements for 
selection are not as rigorous. There are also other provisions relating to regular service such as the 
liability of a member of the service to be transferred, and his being subject to the disciplinary 
jurisdiction of the authorities as prescribed, which the daily-rated workmen are not subjected to. 
They cannot, therefore, be equated with regular workmen for the purposes for their wages. Nor can 
they claim the minimum of the regular pay-scale of the regularly employed” 


Referring to the said legal position the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Haryana and another vs. Tilak Raj and 
others (2003 (6) SCC 23) held that a scale of pay is attached to a definite post and in case of a daily wager, he 
holds no posts. The I Party neither in her pleadings nor in evidence has made out the particular works she 
performed under the II Party, much less any material is placed by her as to the nature of the duties for which she 
was engaged by the II Party. The contention of the I Party in its Statement of Objection that the engagement of the 
I Party was for meeting the office exigencies to attend some unspecified jobs on payment of daily wage for the 
work performed is thus well founded. 


6. In Mohammed Ashif and others vs. State of Bihar and others (200 (5) SCC 475), the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court held that the question of regularization of services of an Employee may arise only in situations where against 
an available clear vacancy an appointment is made on adhoc or on-daily wage basis by an authority competent to 
do so without any artificial break in service. The second situation in which the regularization could be granted is 
held to be where the initial entry of the employee against an available vacancy was found suffering from some 
flaws in the procedure in making the appointment though the person appointing was competent to make such initial 
recruitment and had otherwise followed the procedure prescribed for such recruitment. It is equally held that “the 
all-important condition precedent for such regularization is that the initial entry of such employee must be made 
against the Sanctioned vacancy and by following the Rules and Regulations governing such entry”. 


7. Similarly the constitution bench of the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Karnataka vs. Uma Devi (2006 
(4) SCC ) held that “Jf it is a contractual appointment, the appointment comes to an end at the end of the 
contract, if it were an engagement or appointment on daily wages or casual basis, the same would come to an end 
when it is discontinued. Similarly, a temporary employee could not claim to be made permanent on the expiry of 
his term of appointment. It has also to be clarified that merely because a temporary employee or a casual wage 
worker is continued for a time beyond the term of his appointment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed in 
regular service or made permanent, merely on the strength of such continuance, if the original appointment was 
not made by following a due process of selection as envisaged by the relevant rules. It is not open to the court to 
prevent regular recruitment at the instance of temporary employees whose period of employment has come to an 
end or of ad hoc employees who by the very nature of their appointment, do not acquire any right.” Here in the 
instant case the I party is claiming permanency and seeks for regularization mainly on the so called “Jong duration 
of work” (emphasis supplied) and not on any other valid ground. The dictum quoted above defeats her claim as it 
is bereft of valid support and devoid of merit. 


8. Most of the rulings placed by the I party are not applicable to the facts of the case on hand. The Verdict of 
the Hon’ble High Court of Madras in V Muthukumarasamy and others vs. The Chairman, LIC, Zonal Office 
dated 2.0.2007 also does not get any application in view of the fact involved in that case as the Petitioners 
therein were sponsored by the Employment Exchange and have been appointed on temporary basis from 
shortlisted candidates. As already observed, the I Party herein was not sponsored by Employment Exchange nor 
her engagement was in a clear vacancy by undergoing the Regular Recruitment process. 


9. The I party further relied upon on the ruling of the Hon’ble High Court of Karnataka, Bengaluru in R V 
Mohan Reddy vs. The Chairman, Karnataka Grameena Bank in WP No. 944/2022 (L-RES) dated 
0.02.2025 awarding 60% of Backwages to the Employee from the date of his termination reckoning the two 
decades of service he had under the management as a Peon on daily wage. As against that, the principle laid down 


572 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA AUGUST 6, 2025/SHRAVANA 25, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in a plethora of rulings aforementioned consistently hold that the Casual 
Employment terminates when the same is discontinued, and merely because a temporary or casual worker has been 
engaged beyond the period of his employment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed into regular service or 
made permanent, if the original appointment was not in terms of the process envisaged by the relevant rules. So 
the legal position settled at rest by the Hon’ble Supreme Court disentitles the I party to put forth any claim of 
reinstatement, regularization, continuity of service or back wages with consequential benefits. 


20. To sum up, the solitary materials viz., Ex W-l vouchers show only pay for a single month in the 
respective years and there is no valid material proving that her engagement was continuous in nature and she 
performed duties under the II Party continuously till the date of her disengagement so as to show that her tenure of 
service at a time was more than 240 days in a calendar year and her disengagement was in violation of the 
provisions of Section 25F of the ID Act. So on legal principle and on factual matrix the I Party failed to establish a 
case on merit justifying the relief sought for in the instant Industrial Dispute. Eventually her Claim Petition fails 
and the same is liable to be dismissed. With this view Points No. | to 3 are answered accordingly. 


2I. POINT NO. 4: In view of the above discussion, the I party is held as not entitled for any relief.

The Claim Petition is Dismissed. No order as to cost.

sought for, relied upon various judicial pronouncements of the Hon’ble Apex Court. At the threshold it has to be

of which she claims reinstatement and regularization with continuity of Service and other monetory benefits. In

treated as on a par with persons in regular service of the State of Haryana holding similar posts. 
Daily-rated workers are not required to possess the qualifications prescribed for regular workers, 
nor do they have to fulfil the requirement relating to age at the time of recruitment. They are not 
selected in the manner in which regular employees are selected. In other words the requirements for 
selection are not as rigorous. There are also other provisions relating to regular service such as the 
liability of a member of the service to be transferred, and his being subject to the disciplinary 
jurisdiction of the authorities as prescribed, which the daily-rated workmen are not subjected to.

they claim the minimum of the regular pay-scale of the regularly employed”

I Party was for meeting the office exigencies to attend some unspecified jobs on payment of daily wage for the 
work performed is thus well founded.
